references_named: Robert Morris, Box with the Sound of Its Own Making (1961)
rationale: The recursive sonification of outerHTML is a genuinely web-native gesture: a print cannot read itself, and a recording would betray the point by being made earlier, elsewhere. The mechanism enacts the concept (P1) with unusual fidelity — the script singing its own source is in the source being sung — and Morris is a fresh addition to the canon remix roster, distinct from The Original (downloads source as fake edition) and The webpage going on and off (Creed/timing). The chance/order axis is honestly staged: deterministic mapping of bytes to pitches, yet the melody was never authored. Tone is dry and cheerful-cynic; restraint is real.
reservations: The Morris reference is apt but the broader gesture — code-as-sound self-sonification — sits near a known live-coding/shader-sound neighborhood; the DNA demands novelty of ontology/location, and this work's location (a single page that performs its own runtime) is novel but its core technique is not unprecedented. The black-box visual is clean but minimal; the sound design (square wave, char % 36 mapping) is functional rather than considered as composition. A casual viewer gets the box-humming-itself gag, but the Morris-specific recursion argument may require some wall-text literacy — the double-coding (P7) leans slightly toward the literate end.
revision_suggestion: Consider tightening the double-coding at the surface level: the visual could more directly echo a Morris walnut box (e.g., a literal cube, or an audio waveform-as-object), so the Morris reference lands even before the viewer hears anything. The sound mapping could be made more deliberate — currently a uniform char-to-pitch grid; a more compositional rule (e.g., source-structure aware: tag, attribute, whitespace as distinct sonic classes) would strengthen the 'mechanism is the argument' claim and push toward nuance 5.
